title: Linear Inequalities, Part 3: Traps and the Fast Way

beats.say: In this video, we look at five mistakes students make with inequalities, and then use Desmos to test points in a system and to check a one-variable inequality.
Each trap is shown as a wrong line first, then the right line, with the reason it is so tempting.
Trap one. Dividing both sides of negative six x is at most eighteen by negative six must flip the sign. Students divide correctly but keep the old sign.
Dividing by a negative number flips the inequality. So the correct result is x is greater than or equal to negative three.
Trap two. Only multiplying or dividing by a negative number flips the sign. Some students flip it whenever they see a minus sign anywhere, or when dividing by a positive number.
Multiplying both sides by two, which is positive, keeps the sign the same. So x is greater than six.
Trap three. If b is at most thirty-four point four boxes, students round to the nearest whole number and get thirty-five. But thirty-five boxes would exceed the limit.
The greatest whole number that is still at most thirty-four point four is thirty-four. For greatest, round down, and for least, round up.
Trap four. In a system, a point must satisfy every inequality. A student who solves only the first inequality might say a equals seven is the greatest value, and stop.
The second inequality gives a less than six as well. Both must hold, so the greatest integer is five.
Trap five. At least ten means x can equal ten, so the boundary is included. Some students turn it into a strict inequality.
At least ten means greater than or equal to ten. A strict sign is for words like more than or exceeds.
For a one-variable inequality, algebra is fastest, since it takes two steps and a sign check. Desmos shines for systems of inequalities in two variables.
Our system is y at least x minus three, and y less than negative two x plus sixteen. We want to know which of two points are solutions.
Open a fresh graph. We will type each inequality, and then plot each point we want to test.
Type the first inequality as x minus three is at most y, which is the same as y is at least x minus three. Desmos shades the region above a solid line.
Now type y is less than negative two x plus sixteen. Desmos shades the region below a dashed line.
Where the shaded regions overlap is the solution region. Plot the point five comma four. It lands inside the overlap, so it is a solution.
Now plot the point six comma four. It lands exactly on the dashed boundary, which is not included, so six comma four is not a solution.
Desmos can also check a one-variable inequality. For five minus three x less than seventeen, graph each side as its own curve, and look for where the first is below the second.

card.sub: Where is the first line below?

beats.say: We type the left side as one line, and the right side as another line, and then look at where they cross.
Type y equals five minus three x. This is a line sloping downward.
Now type y equals seventeen. This is a horizontal line, which represents the right side of the inequality.
Click the crossing point. It is at negative four comma seventeen. To the right of negative four, the sloping line is below seventeen, so x greater than negative four is the solution.
Now a practice problem. Solve seven minus two x is at least fifteen. Pause the video, try it, and then watch the solution.
The coefficient of x is negative, so we expect a flip in the last step.
Subtract seven from both sides. Fifteen minus seven is eight, and the sign does not change.
Divide both sides by negative two, and flip the sign. Eight divided by negative two is negative four. So x is at most negative four.
Test a value in the range, x equals negative five. Seven plus ten is seventeen, which is at least fifteen. True. Test a value outside the range, x equals zero. Seven is not at least fifteen. False.
To recap. Flip the sign only when you multiply or divide by a negative number, never otherwise.
Round down for greatest, round up for least, and satisfy every inequality in a system. At least includes the boundary.
beats.item: Round correctly, satisfy all, include boundary

beats.say: Use Desmos to shade systems and test points. In the next unit, we study Advanced Math, starting with equivalent expressions.
